pages.text: The Solar System consists of the Sun and the objects bound to it by gravity. Eight planets orbit the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The four inner planets are rocky terrestrial worlds; the four outer planets are giants. The Sun contains about 99.8 percent of the mass of the Solar System.

Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It has no moons and almost no atmosphere. A day on Mercury, from one sunrise to the next, lasts about 176 Earth days, while its year is only 88 Earth days. Surface temperatures swing from roughly 430 degrees Celsius in daylight to minus 180 degrees Celsius at night.

Venus is the second planet from the Sun and the hottest planet, with a surface temperature near 465 degrees Celsius because of a runaway greenhouse effect in its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere. Venus rotates backwards compared with most planets, and a single rotation takes 243 Earth days, longer than its 225-day year. It has no moons.

Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only place known to support life. About 71 percent of its surface is covered by water. Earth has one natural satellite, the Moon, which orbits at an average distance of about 384,400 kilometres. Earth's atmosphere is mostly nitrogen (78 percent) and oxygen (21 percent).

Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and is often called the Red Planet because iron oxide dust covers its surface. It has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano in the Solar System at about 22 kilometres high. A Martian day is 24 hours and 37 minutes, and its year is about 687 Earth days.

Jupiter is the largest planet, with a mass more than twice that of all the other planets combined. It is a gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium. The Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has persisted for centuries. Jupiter has at least 95 known moons; the four largest, discovered by Galileo in 1610, are Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System.

Saturn is the sixth planet and is famous for its ring system, made mostly of water ice particles ranging from dust grains to boulders. Saturn is the least dense planet; it would float in water if a large enough ocean existed. Its largest moon, Titan, is bigger than Mercury and has a thick nitrogen atmosphere with lakes of liquid methane.

Uranus is the seventh planet and an ice giant. Its axis of rotation is tilted about 98 degrees, so it effectively rolls around the Sun on its side. Uranus was discovered by William Herschel in 1781, the first planet found with a telescope. Its blue-green colour comes from methane in the atmosphere. It has 27 known moons, named after characters from Shakespeare and Pope.

Neptune is the eighth and most distant planet, another ice giant. It was found in 1846 after mathematical predictions by Urbain Le Verrier and John Couch Adams pointed astronomers to its position. Neptune has the strongest winds in the Solar System, reaching about 2,100 kilometres per hour. Its largest moon, Triton, orbits backwards and is probably a captured Kuiper belt object.

Pluto was classified as a planet from its discovery in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh until 2006, when the International Astronomical Union defined the term planet and reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet. Pluto has five known moons; the largest, Charon, is about half Pluto's diameter. The New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto in July 2015.

The asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. Its largest member, Ceres, is about 940 kilometres across and is also classified as a dwarf planet. Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper belt, a ring of icy bodies, and far beyond that the Oort cloud, the hypothesised source of long-period comets.

Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth. The average Earth-Sun distance, about 149.6 million kilometres, is defined as one astronomical unit. Neptune orbits at about 30 astronomical units. The Voyager 1 probe, launched in 1977, crossed into interstellar space in 2012 and is the most distant human-made object.
